clue.text: Still taking in first piece of information

indicators.note: to take something in is to absorb it, so one piece swallows the other

blocks.note: still, as in motionless
1st written with I standing for the digit one

explanation.surface: Someone stands motionless while absorbing their first scrap of news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like the adverb 'yet', but it is the adjective STATIC. 'First' as 1ST, with the figure read as the letter I, is a common crossword trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A statistic is a single numerical fact, one item of data among many.

clue.text: Small share of profits for what's at risk?

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a take is someone's cut of the takings

explanation.surface: An investor wonders whether a tiny cut of the profits justifies the gamble.
explanation.walkthrough: A share of profits also suggests a stake in a business, a neat echo of the answer's other sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A stake is the money a gambler wagers, the sum that could be lost.

clue.text: Buy off a very soft moderate

blocks.note: taken as written
pianissimo, the musical marking for very soft
to ease is to lessen or moderate

explanation.surface: Someone bribes a gentle, middle-of-the-road politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moderate' reads as a noun, a centrist, but it is the verb meaning to lessen. PP is the musical direction pianissimo.
explanation.definitionFit: To buy someone off is to pacify them with concessions, which is exactly to placate or mollify.

clue.text: Bread filling that is dull

indicators.note: a filling sits inside its casing, so one piece goes into the middle of the other

blocks.note: i.e., id est, Latin for 'that is'
nan or naan, the Indian flatbread

explanation.surface: A sandwich filling is judged boring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread filling' looks like a sandwich's contents, but the bread itself does the filling. The abbreviation needs 'that is' together; only 'that' is listed above because 'is' doubles as the link.
explanation.definitionFit: Inane means silly and empty of meaning, close to vapid or tiresome.

clue.text: Dismissal for adding copy into middle of notes she typed

indicators.note: the centre of each word is wanted, so only its central letter is kept
putting one thing into another places it inside

blocks.note: the central letter of this five-letter word
the central letter of this three-letter word
an echo copies a sound
the central letter of this five-letter word

explanation.surface: A secretary is sacked for slipping copied material into the notes she was typing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle of' applies to each of the three words 'notes she typed', giving T, H and P, and ECHO goes between H and P.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting the chop is informal British slang for being sacked from a job.

clue.text: Stopper's team come together for opener

indicators.note: things that come together are joined, so the parts are simply placed side by side

blocks.note: a cork is a bottle stopper, with the possessive S kept
a crew is a team, as of rowers

explanation.surface: A cricket team's fielders gather around their opening batsman.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture is false: a stopper is a bottle cork and the opener is a bottle opener.
explanation.definitionFit: A corkscrew is the spiral tool used to open wine bottles, so it is a kind of opener.

clue.text: Fan removes uniform for closest mate

indicators.note: the clue runs backwards: taking a letter out of the answer is undone by putting it back in

blocks.note: BFF, text-speak for best friend forever
U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A supporter takes off his team kit and gives it to his best friend.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs backwards: the answer, losing its U, leaves BFF, so the solver rebuilds it by putting U into BFF.
explanation.definitionFit: A buff is an enthusiast, as in a film buff or a history buff.

clue.text: How one checked authenticity of old money, then some new

definitions.text: How one checked authenticity of old money, then some new

blocks.clueFragment: How one checked authenticity of old money
blocks.note: surface reading: an old test of a gold piece, done with the teeth
setter's reading: 'and then some' adds a modern currency that is spelt the same as that bite test

explanation.surface: A history of how people once tested coins, with a nod to modern money.
explanation.walkthrough: People once bit a coin to check it was real gold; written as one word, 'bit coin' becomes the digital currency, the 'new' money.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitcoin is a modern digital cryptocurrency, so it is a new kind of money.

clue.text: Play away? It will turn into farce

indicators.note: turning changes the order things face, so these letters get rearranged

blocks.note: the letters as printed

explanation.surface: A worry that an away match will descend into farce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play away' sounds like a sports fixture, but it is British slang for being unfaithful. 'Into' looks like part of the instruction, yet it belongs to the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To play away is an idiom for having an affair, and an affair involves sex outside marriage; the question mark flags the loose fit.

clue.text: Ale and prawn cocktail? It could kill you

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mixture, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pub meal of beer and a prawn cocktail, with a joke about food poisoning.
explanation.walkthrough: Prawn cocktail is a classic British starter, so 'cocktail' looks like part of the dish; it is the signal to mix up the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A military aircraft armed for combat is designed to be lethal, so it could kill.

clue.text: Withdraw sequence of notes

blocks.note: first meaning: to pull back or leave
second meaning: three sol-fa syllables in a row, the second, seventh and second degrees of the scale

explanation.surface: A musician bows out of playing a run of notes.
explanation.walkthrough: The notes are tonic sol-fa syllables (do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti), not letters A to G: RE, TI and RE in a row spell the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To retire is to pull back or leave, as an army retires from a field.

clue.text: Warning given by European after live conflict

definitions.note: the answer is a verb used as a warning, not a noun

indicators.note: coming after means placed later, which fixes the order of the parts

blocks.note: to be is to exist or live
war is armed conflict
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A European issues a warning about living through a war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live' could be the adjective, as in a live broadcast, but here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a cautionary command, as on signs saying 'of the dog', so it serves as a warning.

clue.text: Significant island wrapped by Christo somehow!

indicators.note: what is wrapped sits inside the wrapping, so one piece goes within the other
done somehow means in some unspecified way, so the order is not fixed

blocks.note: I is the abbreviation for island
the name as printed

explanation.surface: The artist Christo, famous for wrapping buildings, wraps an island, a notable event.
explanation.walkthrough: Christo really did wrap islands in fabric (Surrounded Islands, Miami, 1983), so the surface is true; his name supplies most of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Historic describes something important enough to be remembered in history, a landmark event.

clue.text: Abandons the run, gutted to be behind

indicators.note: a gutted thing has had its insides taken out, so only the outer letters remain

blocks.note: first and last letters
first and last letters
first and last letters

explanation.surface: A runner, exhausted, gives up the race and falls behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gutted' looks like British slang for bitterly disappointed, but it empties each of the three words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Astern is the nautical term for towards or at the back of a ship, so it means at the rear.

clue.text: Individual weight of one diamond, perhaps

blocks.note: single means individual or one only
a ton is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A jeweller weighs a single diamond.
explanation.walkthrough: The diamond is not a gem but a playing card: in bridge, a hand holding only one card of a suit holds that card as a lone example.
explanation.definitionFit: In card games, a lone card of its suit in a hand is a singleton; 'perhaps' marks a diamond as one example.

clue.text: Rude man is crazy for nanny

indicators.note: something crazy is out of its right mind and order, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: the letters as printed
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rude man is mad about a nanny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' does double duty in the surface, but its letters belong to the scramble; only 'crazy' signals it.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman employed to look after young children is a nanny, the older name for that job.

clue.text: Annual payment for looking after kids?

blocks.note: p.a., per annum, means yearly
a rental is a sum paid for hire

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a yearly payment is due for childcare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Annual payment' looks like a single phrase; it splits into the abbreviation p.a. and a hire charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Parental describes what mothers and fathers do, and raising and caring for children is their role; the question mark flags the loose adjective.

clue.text: Training is going as intended

blocks.note: first meaning: attending a course of study
second meaning: heading for the planned target

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests training is progressing well; the two halves are separate meanings of one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone attending classes is literally away on a course, and a project on track for its goal is figuratively the same.

clue.text: Abroad for a long time due to lack of services

blocks.note: out, as in out of the country
ages is a long time

explanation.surface: Someone stays abroad a long time because the utilities are not working.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invents a reason to stay away; 'due to' only joins the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: An outage is a period when power, water or another utility supply stops working.

clue.text: Drug best known initially to keep dancers going in trance

definitions.text: Drug best known initially to keep dancers going

blocks.clueFragment: Drug best known initially to keep dancers going
blocks.note: first meaning: the club drug MDMA, often just called E
second meaning: a state of rapture or transport

explanation.walkthrough: 'Trance' is also the dance-music genre of the clubs where this drug is taken, which ties the halves together. 'Initially' hints that its familiar name is a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The club drug MDMA has a street name meaning rapture, and a trance is likewise an overwhelming, rapt state of mind.

clue.text: Shrink gets paler as husband moves back

indicators.note: a spouse's single-letter abbreviation shifts later in the word, a limited rearrangement with nothing added

blocks.note: more white, so paler

explanation.surface: A therapist goes pale as a husband backs away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shrink' looks like the slang for a psychiatrist, but it is the verb. H, the usual abbreviation for husband, moves two places further back, so no new letters arrive.
explanation.definitionFit: To wither is to shrivel and dry up, as a plant does, so it means to shrink.

clue.text: Oven has opening with leather on top

indicators.note: in a down entry, being on top means coming first

blocks.note: to tan is to beat, to give a leathering
a door is an opening into a room

explanation.surface: An oven with a leather-covered door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leather' is the verb, to thrash, not the material; to tan someone's hide means the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A tandoor is the clay oven of Indian and Pakistani cooking, used for tandoori dishes.

clue.text: Properties that provide disappointing rents for the owners

blocks.note: flat, as in a flat, lacklustre performance
an owner lets a property out, while the tenant rents it

explanation.surface: Landlords complain that their buildings bring in poor rent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For the owners' fixes the viewpoint: what a tenant rents, the landlord lets.
explanation.definitionFit: Flatlets are small apartments, a British word for compact rented dwellings.

clue.text: Staff reportedly thriving — except for this bullied Spanish waiter

indicators.note: what is reported is told by word of mouth, so sound matters rather than spelling

blocks.note: to man a post is to staff it
thriving is doing well; said without its first consonant

explanation.surface: Staff are doing fine, except for one Spanish waiter who gets picked on.
explanation.walkthrough: Manuel is the hapless Spanish waiter in the British sitcom Fawlty Towers, bullied by his boss Basil. The sound match is loose: the second half is 'well' with the W dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Manuel, from Barcelona, is the famous put-upon waiter Basil Fawlty constantly abuses in the 1970s comedy.

clue.text: Bring together tips for making ancient thatched cottage homely

indicators.note: a tip is an end point, so the leading letter of each word is wanted

blocks.note: the opening letters of these five words

explanation.surface: Advice on how to bring an old thatched cottage's homely style together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips' looks like advice for decorating, but it means the ends of the words.
explanation.definitionFit: To match things is to pair them up or join them, as in matchmaking.

clue.text: Try reading out opening bits of Secret Agent

indicators.note: the opening of each word is its start, so only leading letters are kept
reading something out says it, so the letter names are spoken

blocks.note: the two leading letters, said by their names one after the other

explanation.surface: Someone attempts to read aloud the start of a spy novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters S and A, said as names, run together into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To essay something is an old, formal verb for attempting it, as in to essay a task.

clue.text: Strong leader for Greeks takes time to make mark

indicators.note: to take something is to hold it, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: the Greek letter matching the opening letter of Strong
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A powerful Greek leader takes his time to make his mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strong leader' is not a strongman but the first letter of 'Strong', given in its Greek form.
explanation.definitionFit: A stigma is a mark of disgrace, and originally a brand burned onto the skin.

clue.text: Share out treatment for serious type of film?

indicators.note: a treatment works something over, so these letters are processed into a new order

blocks.note: the letters as printed

explanation.surface: Splitting up a film treatment, the draft outline of a serious movie.
explanation.walkthrough: A treatment is also a film-industry term for a story outline, which disguises the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthouse cinema means intellectual or experimental films, as opposed to mainstream blockbusters.

clue.text: We're paying for liability

blocks.note: as in 'drinks are on me', footing the bill
the first-person plural pronoun in its object form

explanation.surface: Someone at a bar offers to cover the bill for a debt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On us' is the idiom said when offering to pay, as in 'drinks are on us'; 'We're' supplies the pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: An onus is a burden or responsibility, a duty someone is held to.

clue.text: Boring and reserved, slip inside for a drink

indicators.note: inside means within, so one piece is placed in another

blocks.note: dry, as in a dull, dry lecture
shy means reserved
to err is to slip up

explanation.surface: A dull, quiet person sneaks in for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slip inside' reads as nipping into a pub, but 'slip' is a mistake that goes inside the reserved word.
explanation.definitionFit: Dry sherry, such as fino, is a fortified wine from Spain served as an aperitif.
